title: Checkpoint: The Islamic World and the East
objective: After this level you can explain how learning and trade flowed between the Islamic world, China and Europe.
summary: Learning and trade flowed both ways: paper and numerals west, Greek learning into Arabic and Latin, Chinese inventions west and Islamic science east. A 751-1325 timeline.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: knowledge travelled both ways along the same roads.
cards.body: Under the Mongol peace, Chinese inventions went west while Islamic science went east. Let’s put the whole chapter on one page.

cards.headline: The Islamic world and the East, in order

events.label: Al-Mansur founds Baghdad, the Round City
The Diamond Sutra is printed in China
Ibn Battuta sets out from Tangier

cards.headline: Two-way traffic
cards.body: Look at what moved. Papermaking came west through Samarkand, Baghdad made paper by the 790s, and it reached Europe through Sicily and Spain by the 12th century. Numbers came from India and reached Europe through mathematicians of the Islamic world. Greek books went into Arabic in Baghdad, and Ibn Sina’s Canon went into Latin for Europe’s doctors. Under the Pax Mongolica, Chinese papermaking, printing, gunpowder and the compass spread west, while Islamic astronomy, mathematics and medicine spread east. Not sealed rooms: a crossroads.

mascot.line: Seven chapters in, and the map just got a lot bigger. Well travelled!

questions.prompt: In the story of the Islamic world and the East, where did the digits we use today originate?

options.label: Arabia
options.rationale: Arabia carried them; India invented them.

options.label: Greece
options.rationale: The Greeks used letters as numbers.

options.label: China
options.rationale: Paper came from China, not the digits.

questions.explanation: The Hindu-Arabic numerals originated in India in the 6th or 7th century.

questions.prompt: Under the Pax Mongolica, which way did knowledge move between China, the Islamic world and Europe?

options.label: It stopped, because the roads closed
options.rationale: The roads were safer than before.

options.label: Both ways: inventions west, Islamic science east

questions.explanation: Chinese inventions spread west while Islamic astronomy, mathematics and medicine spread east.

questions.prompt: Islamic medicine reached Europe: which book was a European medical textbook until the mid-17th century?
questions.explanation: Ibn Sina’s Canon served as a medical textbook in Europe until the mid-17th century.

questions.prompt: The Islamic world and the East: what ended the Abbasid caliphate whose Baghdad had sponsored Greek translations?

The Battle of Talas in 751

options.label: The Silk Road closing to trade
A revolt led by the Umayyads
